title: Revisiting the XMM-Newton Observations of the Galactic Microquasar SS 433: Implications for the Origin of the Ultrahigh-Energy Emission Detected by LHAASO
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures; submitted to The Astrophysical Journal (currently under review)
summary: Recently, the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) detected ultrahigh-energy (UHE; photon energy E>100TeV) $γ$-ray emission toward SS 433, the microquasar embedded in the W50 nebula, making it a promising Galactic PeVatron candidate. We reanalyze the archival XMM-Newton observations covering the bipolar jets and the thermal X-ray shell north of SS 433, and derive spatially resolved profiles of the nonthermal X-ray intensity and photon index along both jets. The jet emission softens with distance from the source, implying a correspondingly evolving electron population. In particular, a hard electron component appears close to the jet bases, which can account for the UHE emission from SS 433 via inverse Compton radiation if the magnetic field remains approximately uniform along the jets. The result, however, is highly sensitive to the magnetic field profile. For flux-conserving configurations in which the field decreases as the jet expands, the stronger field required in the inner regions may reduce the number of X-ray-emitting electrons and suppress their inverse Compton emission. Furthermore, electron transport calculations show that injection only at the jet bases cannot reproduce the observed intensity and spectral evolution, particularly the downstream re-brightening features, indicating additional particle injection and/or re-acceleration within the jets.

AI.tldr: Analysis of archival XMM-Newton data on SS 433 reveals spatially resolved nonthermal X-ray spectra along the bipolar jets that soften with distance, implying evolving electron populations. A hard electron component near the jet bases can explain LHAASO's UHE gamma-ray emission via inverse Compton radiation if the magnetic field stays roughly uniform; however, the result is highly sensitive to the magnetic field profile. Electron transport modeling shows that jet-base injection alone cannot reproduce the observed downstream re-brightening, requiring additional in-jet particle injection or re-acceleration.
AI.motivation: LHAASO recently detected ultrahigh-energy (>100 TeV) gamma-ray emission from the microquasar SS 433, making it a strong Galactic PeVatron candidate. This paper aims to connect the observed UHE emission to the nonthermal X-ray properties of the jets by reanalyzing archival XMM-Newton data and testing whether the jet electron population can account for the UHE gamma-rays via inverse Compton radiation.
AI.method: The authors reanalyze archival XMM-Newton observations covering SS 433's bipolar jets and the thermal X-ray shell north of the source. They extract spatially resolved profiles of nonthermal X-ray intensity and photon index along both jets, then compare these with expectations from inverse Compton emission using various magnetic field configurations. They also perform electron transport calculations to test whether jet-base injection alone can reproduce the observed intensity and spectral evolution.
AI.result: The jet X-ray emission softens with distance from the source, indicating evolving electron populations. A hard electron component is found near the jet bases, which can account for the UHE emission via inverse Compton if the magnetic field is approximately uniform along the jets. However, the result strongly depends on the magnetic field profile; in flux-conserving configurations where the field decreases with jet expansion, the stronger inner fields suppress the inverse Compton emission. Transport calculations show injection only at the jet bases cannot reproduce observed downstream features like re-brightening.
AI.conclusion: SS 433's UHE gamma-ray emission can potentially be explained by inverse Compton radiation from high-energy electrons near the jet bases, but only under uniform magnetic field assumptions. The observed downstream re-brightening and spectral evolution indicate that particle injection or re-acceleration must also occur within the jets themselves, not solely at the jet bases.

title: Iron K$α$ signatures from accretion disks around fermionic dark matter cores
comment: Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics. Comments are welcome
summary: The fluorescent iron line and its broadening due to relativistic effects are excellent probes to study the inner part of an accretion disk and the space-time geometry near the compact object. We investigate the iron K$α$ line profile within the extended RAR model, which describes a fermionic dark matter distribution on galaxy scales. The most general solutions are characterized by a compact and highly degenerate core able to mimic the central black hole, transitioning into an extended halo composed of the same particles. We aim to contrast the resulting line morphologies in this scenario with those predicted by the standard Kerr black hole paradigm. Special attention will be given to MCG-06-30-15 galaxy. We compute the line profile using the numerical ray-tracing code, Skylight. We consider two distinct configurations for the emissivity of the cold accretion disk: an irradiation profile based on the lamp-post corona prescription, and a phenomenological power-law profile. The resulting profiles exhibit a diverse phenomenology. In particular, the most compact fermion cores produce a line broadening comparable to that observed in rapidly rotating black holes. The presence of emitting matter at radii smaller than a gravitational radius yields distinctive spectral features that are entirely absent in the black hole scenario. For MCG-06-30-15 galaxy, we find a good agreement with the observed broad features of the iron line profile, provided the compactness of the fermion core is close to critical. These results reinforce the need for independent black hole spin measurements. Combined with such constraints, iron-line spectroscopy may provide a powerful observational tool to distinguish black holes from alternative compact solutions, in particular compact fermionic dark-matter cores.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates iron Kα line profiles in the extended RAR (Ruffini-Argüelles-Rueda) model, where fermionic dark matter forms compact degenerate cores that mimic black holes surrounded by extended halos. Using the Skylight ray-tracing code, the authors compute line morphologies for two emissivity prescriptions and compare them to standard Kerr black hole predictions, focusing on the galaxy MCG-06-30-15.
AI.motivation: To test whether alternative compact objects—specifically compact fermionic dark-matter cores in the RAR model—can produce relativistic iron line broadening similar to that attributed to black holes, and to identify spectral signatures that could distinguish such alternatives from standard Kerr black holes.
AI.method: The authors use the numerical ray-tracing code Skylight to compute relativistic iron Kα line profiles in the extended RAR model spacetime. They consider two accretion disk emissivity prescriptions: a lamp-post corona irradiation profile and a phenomenological power-law profile, and compare the resulting line shapes to the standard Kerr black hole scenario.
AI.result: The most compact fermion cores produce line broadening comparable to rapidly rotating Kerr black holes. Emitting matter at radii smaller than the gravitational radius yields spectral features absent in the black hole scenario. For MCG-06-30-15, good agreement with observed broad iron line features is found when the fermion core compactness is near critical.
AI.conclusion: Iron-line spectroscopy combined with independent black hole spin measurements can serve as a powerful observational discriminator between Kerr black holes and alternative compact solutions, particularly compact fermionic dark-matter cores within the RAR framework.

title: Thermal evolution of neo-neutron stars. II. Temperature-dependent crusts
comment: 10 pages, 11 figures, 1 table; submitted to A&A
summary: The neo-neutron star phase is an intermediate stage in the evolution from a hot lepton-rich compact object, which is formed in the aftermath of a core-collapse supernova or an accretion-induced collapse of a white dwarf, to a cold deleptonized neutron star (NS). Alternatively, this phase can occur after a binary NS merger if the final compact object does not collapse immediately into a black hole. Radial temperature profiles provided by numerical simulations of proto-NS evolution suggest that the composition and mechanical structure of the star's core at the beginning of the neo-NS phase are, as a good approximation, identical to those of a cold NS. In contrast, the composition and mechanical structure of the outer layers (i.e., the crust) are expected to change as the star cools. The thermal evolution of neo-NSs with temperature-dependent (inner) envelopes was considered by Beznogov et al. (2020). Here, we investigated what happens if the equation of state (EoS) of the entire crust, including its composition, depends on temperature. We analyzed the thermal, mechanical, and chemical evolution of neo-NSs by further developing and employing neo-NSCool, our NS thermal evolution code. First, we proved that thermally dripped neutrons slightly slow down the cooling during the early thermal relaxation stage. Then, we showed that the EoSs with exotic light species in the deepest layers of the crust result in significantly slower cooling in the photon cooling era compared with the EoSs that favor massive nuclei. The crust's composition also impacts the crystallization process as well as the way in which the crust contracts while it cools. The EoSs with light nuclei cause the innermost layers to remain liquid for a longer time than the EoSs with heavy nuclei.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the thermal, mechanical, and chemical evolution of neo-neutron stars by incorporating temperature-dependent equations of state for the entire crust into the neo-NSCool simulation code. The authors show that thermally dripped neutrons slow early cooling, EoSs with exotic light species significantly slow cooling in the photon era, and crust composition affects crystallization and contraction timescales.
AI.motivation: Previous work by Beznogov et al. (2020) considered temperature-dependent envelopes in neo-NS thermal evolution, but the crust's equation of state and composition were assumed temperature-independent. This paper aims to understand how a temperature-dependent crust EoS—including its composition—affects the thermal, mechanical, and chemical evolution of neo-neutron stars.
AI.method: The authors extend the neo-NSCool code, their neutron star thermal evolution code, to include temperature-dependent equations of state for the entire crust. They simulate the thermal, mechanical, and chemical evolution of neo-NSs and compare outcomes for different crustal EoSs (those with exotic light species vs. those favoring massive nuclei), examining cooling rates, crystallization, and crustal contraction.
AI.result: (1) Thermally dripped neutrons slightly slow down cooling during the early thermal relaxation stage. (2) EoSs with exotic light species in the deepest crustal layers result in significantly slower cooling in the photon cooling era compared to EoSs favoring massive nuclei. (3) Crust composition affects crystallization, with EoSs containing light nuclei causing the innermost crustal layers to remain liquid longer than EoSs with heavy nuclei, and also influences how the crust contracts during cooling.
AI.conclusion: The temperature dependence of the crust's equation of state and composition has important consequences for neo-neutron star cooling, crystallization, and structural evolution. Crustal EoSs with light exotic species substantially alter cooling behavior compared to those with massive nuclei, and the composition dictates how long the inner crust remains liquid.

title: Probing Axion Like Particle-Proton Interactions through the Interplay of Dark Matter and Cosmic Rays in Large-Scale Structure
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures
summary: Axion-like particles (ALPs) provide a well-motivated dark matter candidate whose interactions with Standard Model particles may generate observable cosmological signatures. We investigate the diffuse $γ$-ray emission produced by the scattering process between ALP dark matter and cosmic-ray (CR) protons inside dark matter halos, and explore its detectability through the cross-correlation between the unresolved $γ$-ray background (UGRB) measured by \textit{Fermi} Large Area Telescope (LAT) and the Two Micron All Sky Survey Redshift Survey (2MRS) galaxy catalog in the local Universe ($z\leq0.1$). To model the cosmological $\mathrm{GeV}$-$\mathrm{PeV}$ CR proton population, we develop a phenomenological bottom-up prescription that links CR injection to the star formation rate through the supernova rate, while the steady-state CR density is determined by diffusive escape. Our forecasts indicate that UGRB-galaxy cross-correlation measurements can probe previously unexplored regions of the ALP parameter space over a broad range of ALP masses. More generally, this work presents a general framework for cosmological observables generated by interactions between dark matter and an additional astrophysical field, opening a new avenue for indirect dark matter searches using large-scale structure observations.

They develop a phenomenological bottom-up prescription linking CR proton injection to star formation rate via supernova rate, with steady-state CR density determined by diffusive escape. title: First fast radio burst search campaign at the Argentine Institute of Radio Astronomy
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are intense millisecond-duration radio transients of extragalactic origin whose physical nature remains under active investigation, and which also serve as probes of the intergalactic medium. We report on the first FRB search campaign carried out at the Argentine Institute of Radio Astronomy (IAR) between December 2024 and March 2026, targeting nearby galaxy superclusters in the southern sky. We observed fields in the Ophiuchus, Shapley, and Sculptor/Phoenix supercluster regions with one of the two 30~m antennas of the IAR, using a ROACH-based backend with 400~MHz of bandwidth centred at 1400~MHz and a time resolution of 41--82~$μ$s, for a total net observing time of 212~h. The data were searched for dispersed single pulses with \texttt{PRESTO} in the dispersion measure range $100 \leq \mathrm{DM} \leq 500$, and candidates were classified with the FETCH machine learning classifier. The pipeline was validated on archival Parkes data containing known FRBs and on synthetic bursts injected into IAR observations. One FRB candidate, FRB~20251018, was identified on 18 October 2025 in an observation pointed towards the galaxy cluster A2870, in the Phoenix supercluster, with a dispersion measure of $243$, a signal-to-noise ratio of 8.2, and a FETCH probability of $p=0.99$. To the best of our knowledge, this would be the first FRB detected from South America. A set of more marginal candidates is also presented. These results demonstrate the capability of the IAR antennas to detect FRBs and support the continuation and extension of the monitoring campaign, including coincident dual-antenna observations and cross-matches with gravitational-wave events and electromagnetic transients.

After 212 hours of observations, the pipeline identified one FRB candidate (FRB 20251018) with a dispersion measure of 243, marking the first FRB detected from South America.
AI.motivation: FRBs remain poorly understood astrophysical transients, and their detection from southern hemisphere facilities—particularly using smaller antennas—can help constrain their nature and use them as intergalactic medium probes. The authors aim to demonstrate that IAR's 30 m antennas are capable of detecting FRBs, expanding the observational coverage of the southern sky.

Data were searched for dispersed single pulses with PRESTO (DM range 100–500), and candidates were classified using the FETCH machine learning classifier. The pipeline was validated on archival Parkes FRB data and synthetic burst injections.
AI.result: One FRB candidate (FRB 20251018) was detected on 18 October 2025 toward galaxy cluster A2870 in the Phoenix supercluster, with DM=243, S/N=8.2, and FETCH probability p=0.99—the first FRB from South America. Several more marginal candidates were also reported.
AI.conclusion: The IAR antennas are demonstrated to be capable of detecting FRBs, supporting the continuation and extension of the monitoring campaign, including dual-antenna coincident observations and cross-matches with gravitational-wave events and other electromagnetic transients.
